facts.says: Hans is a servant of Duke Horacio at Lumbridge Castle.
Hans spends his days walking round and round the castle courtyard, and has done for longer than anyone remembers.
His walk goes clockwise round the courtyard, and a lap takes him about a minute.
Hans watches the newcomers arrive in Lumbridge, eager for adventure, and remembers each of them, down to how long they've been about in the world.
When someone's lost, Hans tells them they're in Lumbridge Castle in Misthalin, that the road over the river runs north to Varrock, and that Draynor Village lies to the west.
Anyone looking for whoever's in charge gets sent by Hans up to the Duke's study on the first floor.
Hans frightens easily: threaten the castle and he runs off screaming for help.
Years later, Hans still panics at the memory of the stranger who once came in threatening to kill everyone in the castle.
One Christmas the Duke gave Hans a chair from his own room, and Hans was overjoyed to rest his aching feet at last.
Treasure hunters with clue scrolls are sometimes sent to find Hans, and he hands them their next clue or a casket.
When part of the castle cellar wall fell in, Hans had to spend all day clearing up, and the Duke says it was an earthquake.
Hans is delighted to have the cave goblins as new neighbours under the castle, though he knows not everyone in Lumbridge liked the peace treaty.
Horacio is the Duke of Lumbridge and rules the town and the land around it from Lumbridge Castle.
The Duke lives on the castle's first floor, in the northern bedroom.
The Duke says he can't leave his castle unattended, so he sends others on his errands.
The Duke is a follower of Saradomin and swears by him.
Asked where the money is, the Duke says he's heard blacksmiths do well for themselves among the peasantry.
The Duke's household turned up a curious old talisman while sorting through things stored in the castle cellar, and he has an odd feeling it matters.
The Duke wants the talisman taken to Archmage Sedridor at the Wizards' Tower, across the bridge from Draynor Village, as the wizards have been hunting for magical artefacts.
The talisman the Duke sent to the Wizards' Tower helped the wizards find their lost way back to a hidden rune essence mine.
In the Duke's father's day Crandor was as important as Falador or Varrock, but when the Duke was little all word from it suddenly stopped.
The Duke's father was so afraid of the dragon Elvarg that he posted lookouts on the castle roof.
The Duke keeps anti-dragon shields, but he hasn't an endless supply and gives one only for a truly worthy cause.
When the player said they meant to slay Elvarg, the Duke judged them up to it and handed over one of his anti-dragon shields.
The player slew Elvarg on Crandor, and the Duke now lets them have a dragon shield whenever they ask.
The Duke insists the castle cellar wall fell in because of an earthquake, and he's waiting on builders to mend it.
The Duke holds that goblins live in natural caves and haven't the wit to dig tunnels of their own.
The Duke signed a peace treaty with Ur-tag of the Dorgeshuun: above ground is Lumbridge's, below ground is the cave goblins', except the town's cellars.
The Duke chose to leave the hole in the castle cellar open, as a road for trade with the cave goblins.

The Duke threw his adviser Sigmund out of his service for hiding the castle silverware to start a war with the cave goblins; he'd known Sigmund was in HAM, which he disapproves of but says isn't against the law.
The Duke grants the trading permits in Lumbridge, and the Groats family hold the one for milk.
The Duke hosts a secret council of leaders from across the lands at Lumbridge Castle, from the White Knights' Sir Amik Varze to Pirate Pete and the ogre Skrach.
At the council's feast the Duke was whisked away by a strange old man moments before the Culinaromancer froze his guests in time.
The Cook is the head cook of Lumbridge Castle and works in the kitchen on its ground floor.
The Cook wears standard cook's issue, a plain hat, apron and stripey trousers, and is put out if anyone doubts he's a real cook.
The Cook says he has a wife, four children and a goat to look after.
Running off to sea as a pirate is out for the Cook: his wife gets seasick and he has an irrational fear of eyepatches.
The Duke doesn't allow holidays for his core staff, the Cook included.
The Cook gets his flour from Millie at Mill Lane Mill and his eggs from the Groats' farm across the river, where Gillie Groats looks after the dairy cows.
Only the big cheeses get to dine at the Duke's table, never the people who fetch the ingredients.
The Cook has admitted that every cake he's ever tried has burned, which is why he keeps sending adventurers for more ingredients.
The Cook is in a terrible state: it's the Duke's birthday, he forgot to buy the cake ingredients, and he's sure he'll be sacked and thrown into the street.
For the cake the Cook needs a bucket of milk, an egg and a pot of flour.
The player brought the Cook his milk, egg and flour, and he declared himself saved.
The Cook's range is the Cook-o-matic, which uses temperature control and magic, and the salesman promised it burns less food.
Since the player helped with the cake, the Cook lets them use his own range; before that he'd chase them off it.
When the cellar wall fell in, rock dust went everywhere in the kitchen and got on all the Cook's ingredients.
The Cook's ancestor, the great chef Franizzard Van Lumbcook, cooked a banquet at the castle a century ago so fine that he and all his descendants were given a job for life.
The Cook has always felt he owes his job to his ancestor rather than his own cooking, and longs to prove he's a great cook too.
The Cook has owned up that it was never really the Duke's birthday; he doesn't even know when it is, and he was testing whether the player could be trusted.
The Cook is recreating his ancestor's banquet from an ancient cookbook that calls for odd things: an eye of newt, a rotten tomato, greenman's ale and a Dirty Blast, a fruit blast with ash in it.
The Cook's old recipe let the Culinaromancer into the feast, and the Cook can't believe he nearly got all those people killed before the player defeated him.
Father Aereck is the priest of Saradomin who looks after the church of Lumbridge.
Lumbridge church was built more than two hundred and thirty years ago, and Aereck is proud of it.
Aereck took over as Lumbridge's priest after Father Urhney left to pray and meditate in the swamp.
Aereck's old friend Father Urhney lives as a hermit in a shack in the far west of Lumbridge Swamp, and Aereck calls him the expert on ghosts.
Urhney says that when the two of them were trainee priests, Aereck kept getting stuck up the bell ropes.
Aereck holds that Saradomin has more followers than any other god, at least in this part of the world, and can't believe anyone hasn't heard of him.
Aereck teaches that Saradomin made the world together with his brothers Guthix and Zamorak.
Aereck supposes that anything not from this world is all slime and tentacles.
Aereck had always taken the old stories of a war between the gods as a symbol of the struggle between light and darkness in people's hearts.
A ghost is haunting the church graveyard, and Aereck wants someone to get rid of it.
Aereck heard that a warlock had stolen the graveyard ghost's skull, and he hates warlocks.
The player got rid of the graveyard ghost, and Aereck asks Saradomin to smile on them for it.
Aereck admits he only ever had the one quest to give.
The Wise Old Man of Draynor sometimes sends Aereck a letter by an adventurer, and Aereck rewards whoever brings it.
Aereck hopes the cave goblins under Lumbridge, who have lived in darkness so long, will come into the light of Saradomin.
Fred keeps sheep at a farmhouse north-west of Lumbridge, south of the windmill and beside the sheep pen.
Fred is a well-fed looking farmer.
Fred meets every visitor by demanding to know what they're doing on his land.
Somebody keeps leaving Fred's gates open and letting all his sheep out, and he suspects passing strangers.
Fred won't have anyone looking for things to kill on his farm, and calls such folk scoundrels.
Fred can't see how anyone gets lost near his farm: follow the road east and south and you're in Lumbridge.
Fred fears The Thing in his fields, which nobody has ever properly seen: some say it's a black-hearted shapeshifter after the souls of decent folk, others say it's just a sheep.
Onions grow on Fred's farm, next to the sheep field, and folk come by for them.
Fred keeps only a few chickens; Seth Groats, on the other farm over the river towards Varrock, has loads.
Fred lends out shears and warns that some sheep don't like being sheared, so persistence is the key.
The nearest spinning wheel, Fred says, is on the first floor of Lumbridge Castle, just east along the road from his house.
Fred's sheep are getting mighty woolly, and he wants someone to shear them and spin the wool into balls for him.
Fred wants twenty balls of wool, and he's promised some sort of payment for them.
The player sheared Fred's sheep and brought him the wool, and he paid up, if a little grudgingly.
The player keeps telling Fred that penguins disguised as sheep are up to something; Fred is a sheep farmer, and he thinks they've been hearing voices.
Fred was dismayed to hear HAM fanatics were holding Jimmy the Chisel, and admits he's just a farmer with no idea how to deal with fanatics.
Fred was full of thanks once the player sorted out the business with Jimmy the Chisel.
The Wise Old Man, whose real name is Dionysius, is a famous old adventurer and wizard of Saradomin who has settled in a house in Draynor Village.
He'd rather you left out the 'old' and called him a sage.
In his time he has delved the deadliest dungeons, roamed the jungles of Karamja, meditated on Entrana, crossed the desert to Menaphos and Sophanem, and read dusty tomes in Varrock's library.
He offers to look through adventurers' banks and tell them which old quest junk they can chuck away.
He gives out little jobs rather than quests: bronze bars, beer, leather cowls against the hail, and bread, since he has no decent larder.

He sends adventurers off with letters to old friends: Father Aereck, Reldo the librarian, Thurgo the dwarf, Abbot Langley, the Oracle on Ice Mountain and Father Lawrence, whom he hears is drinking too much.
He wears a blue partyhat and spectacles, is very fond of the hat, and won't part with it for anyone.
Draynor bank was robbed, and the guard outside will show anyone a recording of the robbery that shows the Wise Old Man doing it.
Accused of robbing the bank, he protests that he's an old man who walks with a stick, and tells people not to worry about him or his finances.
He grumbles that a lifetime of saving villages earned him nothing but a freezing old house next to a pig-sty, among yobs who can't keep their hands off the market stalls.
He keeps a telescope pointed at the Wizards' Tower, and says he simply admires its architecture.
He says money is terribly important when you haven't enough of it, but once you have as much as he has, it doesn't matter.
He holds there are three gods, Saradomin, Guthix and Zamorak, and gets very cross at talk of any others.
He hasn't been on what you'd call a quest in a long while.
His last adventure was defending the Piscatoris Fishing Colony from sea trolls, where the Sea Troll Queen laid him low and the player finished her off.
Since then he says he's retired from adventuring: he's an old man, and new times need new heroes.
To the player alone, he has hinted he might rob again, calling the bank job a shopping trip rather than a quest.
He once played dead in a mahogany coffin to fool the troll Mother, whose band he'd driven out of the tunnels in his youth, and gave the game away by snoring.
He came with other heroes to help the player against Galvek's dragons, and cheered when Galvek fell.
He says he knew Queen Ellamaria long before she married King Roald, when she was a barmaid at the Blue Moon Inn.
Aggie is a witch who lives in Draynor Village, in a house off a dead-end road on the village's east side.
Aggie mostly makes whatever she finds pretty, and makes dyes to brighten up the women's clothes.
Aggie makes red dye from redberries, yellow dye from onions and blue dye from woad leaves, for a few coins a time.
Aggie picks her redberries in the woods south of Varrock, and the food shop in Port Sarim sometimes has them.
Aggie thinks yellow a strange colour to come by, since it comes from onion skins, and sends people to the farm east of Draynor, by the sheep field, for onions.
Woad leaves are hard to find; Aggie's customers tell her the chief gardener in Falador grows them.
Aggie hasn't turned anyone into a frog in years.
Aggie blames talking chickens, and the flying fish of a few years back, on the professor's menace of a machine in the manor north of the village.
Call Aggie names and she waves her hands and takes a few coins from your purse as a fine, or a pot of flour if you have one.
Aggie warns that anyone who insults a witch never knows what shape they might wake up in.
Aggie's skin paste, mixed from ash, flour, water and redberries in her cauldron, is one of her most popular potions with people who want to pretty up their faces.
Aggie mutters strange words over the cauldron as she mixes, and reckons her paste will make you look good at the Varrock dances.
Aggie claims she once made a tomato by accident while trying to summon a lesser demon, and that tomatoes do sometimes bite.
Aggie's new apprentice, Jimmy the Chisel, went to Lumbridge for supplies and hasn't come back, and she's worried sick but can't leave until he returns.
Jimmy the Chisel is back with Aggie, safe and sound, and she was happy to repay the favour.
The skin paste Aggie mixed for the player helped disguise Prince Ali when he escaped from Lady Keli.
Aggie can take the dye out of poorly made clothes using something from the gut of a Hemenster whitefish, which only bites on slimy eels.
Aggie says black dye is easy, ground from black mushrooms, but there's no such thing as white dye.
Ned is an old sailor who lives in a small house in the east of Draynor Village.
Ned was a man of the sea, but he says those days are behind him now.
Ned sells rope, or makes you one from balls of wool, under the name Ned's Handmade Rope, all wool.
Ned insists you can make strong rope from wool, and gets short with anyone who mentions hemp or jute.
Ned says an old sailor needs his money for a little drop of rum.
Ned boasts he has fought monsters that would turn your hair blue, and won't be laughed at for getting old.
Ned is no member of a sewing circle and won't knit sweaters, though he'll make a wool wig or stitch arrow holes in a shirt.
To Ned a ship will always beat dry land, however long he lives ashore, and he loves the salt spray on his face.
Nobody will give Ned work at sea any more; they say he's too old.
Ned would sail anywhere for the chance to captain a ship once more.
Ned captained the Lady Lumbridge to Crandor for the player, and the dragon wrecked her on the island.
Ned says he got home from Crandor towed by a passing friendly whale.
Ned will happily sail the player to Crandor again, and promises to steer a little better this time.
Ned made the wool wig that helped disguise Prince Ali when he escaped from Lady Keli.
Ned has been talking about strange goings-on in the ruined building full of goblins and spiders between Draynor and Lumbridge.
Ned's rope really comes from Neitiznot, traded for balls of wool, because his fingers aren't nimble enough any more; the player knows and has promised to keep quiet.
Ned has a sweetheart on the Fremennik Isles, Jofridr, who knows him as her Neddie, and he means to visit her soon.
Morgan lives in a house in Draynor Village, just north of Ned's.
Morgan always looks scared.
Morgan keeps garlic in a cupboard upstairs, just in case Count Draynor comes and tries anything.
Morgan points out that the village is even named after the Count.
Morgan has studied the legends: Count Draynor came long ago from dark lands in the east and built Draynor Manor, and many who tried to slay him failed.
Morgan is convinced the vampyre Count Draynor, in the manor to the north, must be stopped once and for all.
Morgan admits the Count hasn't left his manor or attacked the village in generations, certainly not since Morgan moved here, but asks what happens if he starts again.
Hardly anyone else in Draynor is afraid of the Count, and Morgan thinks them fools for it.
Morgan has hoped for a long time that a bold adventurer would come and deal with the Count.
Morgan has heard of a retired vampyre hunter, Dr Harlow, a bit of an old soak who spends his days in the Blue Moon Inn in Varrock.
Morgan has read that vampyres are not killed easily, and only someone with the right skills and kit stands a chance.
The player staked Count Draynor, and Morgan says the village can finally live without fear.
Every time they meet, Morgan thanks the player again for slaying the vampyre and calls them a hero.
